claim: Mirror neurons were discovered in 1992 in ventral premotor cortical area F5 of macaque monkeys.
source: Mirror neurons (MNs) were discovered in 1992 in ventral premotor cortical area F5 of macaque monkeys (di Pellegrino et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to di Pellegrino et al., 1992

claim: Mirror neurons discharged both when the monkey made active movements and when it observed specific meaningful actions performed by the experimenter.
source: They received their name in 1996 when they were introduced by Gallese and colleagues as neurons that " (...) discharged both when the monkey made active movements and when it observed specific meaningful actions performed by the experimenter." (Gallese et al., 1996, p. 595).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallese et al., 1996

claim: Many mirror neurons seemed to prefer the same action during observation and execution.
source: In addition, many of these neurons seemed to prefer the same action during observation and execution.
evidence: Based on inference from previous findings mentioned in the introduction

claim: Mirror neurons might be important for imitating or understanding an observed action.
source: This eventually led to the interpretation that 'motor' neurons were found that might be important for imitating (Rizzolatti et al., 2001) or understanding an observed action (Gallese et al., 1996; Rizzolatti et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rizzolatti et al., 2001; Gallese et al., 1996; Rizzolatti et al., 1996

claim: Neurons with similar properties to mirror neurons were found in other brain regions and in other species, including humans.
source: In subsequent years, neurons with similar properties were found in other brain regions and in other species, including humans (Fogassi et al., 2005; Mukamel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fogassi et al., 2005; Mukamel et al., 2010

claim: There are specific mirror neuron networks for actions, emotions, and vitality, each involving multiple brain regions.
source: More recently, it has been proposed that there are specific mirror neuron networks for actions, emotions, and vitality, each involving multiple brain regions (Rizzolatti and Sinigaglia, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rizzolatti and Sinigaglia, 2016

claim: A mirror mechanism transforms sensory representations of others' behaviour into one's own motor or visceromotor representations concerning that behaviour.
source: As defined by Rizzolatti and Sinigaglia, 2016, p. 757, a mirror mechanism " (…) transforms sensory representations of others' behaviour into one's own motor or visceromotor representations concerning that behaviour.".
evidence: Supported by citation to Rizzolatti and Sinigaglia, 2016

claim: The term 'mirror mechanism' is not uniformly understood.
source: It should be noted that the term 'mirror mechanism' is not uniformly understood (e.g. compare Bonini et al., 2022 and Rizzolatti and Sinigaglia, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonini et al., 2022 and Rizzolatti and Sinigaglia, 2016

claim: The definition of mirror neurons by Gallese et al., 1996 does not require a shared code.
source: However, the definition of MNs by Gallese et al., 1996 does not require a shared code (e.g., Cook and Bird, 2013; Csibra, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cook and Bird, 2013; Csibra, 2005

claim: For more than 90% of mirror neurons, a visual-motor congruence was reported, which could be strict (31.5%) or broad (60.9%).
source: For more than 90% of the MNs, a so-called visual-motor congruence was reported, which could be strict (31.5%) or broad (60.9%).
evidence: Based on inference from Gallese et al., 1996 study mentioned in the text

claim: The action-observation-related responses of many F5 mirror neurons can be influenced by the spatial relationship of the observer to the observed action.
source: Doubts about the existence of a shared action code arise by subsequent studies that showed that the action-observation-related responses of many F5 MNs can be influenced by a number of factors like the spatial relationship of the observer to the observed action (Caggiano et al., 2011; Caggiano et al., 2009; Maranesi et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Caggiano et al., 2011; Caggiano et al., 2009; Maranesi et al., 2017

claim: In some mirror neurons the direction of discharge rate modulation is opposite during execution and observation.
source: and that in some MNs the direction of discharge rate modulation is opposite during execution and observation (Kraskov et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kraskov et al., 2009

claim: Two rhesus macaques were trained to perform the behavioral paradigm.
source: Two rhesus macaques were trained to perform the behavioral paradigm depicted in Figure 1.
evidence: Describes the experimental subjects used in the study

claim: The paradigm consisted of two tasks: an execution task and an observation task.
source: The paradigm consisted of two tasks that were performed in two separate blocks (Figure 1A): an execution task, in which the experimental monkey had to perform one out of three possible actions on objects with identical visual appearance (Figure 1B, top row), and an observation task, in which he had to observe the same actions carried out by a human actor in front of him (Figure 1B, bottom row).
evidence: Describes the experimental design with reference to Figure 1

claim: Each object could be either lifted, twisted clockwise or shifted rightwards.
source: Each object was mechanically set up to allow only one of the three actions: it could be either lifted, twisted clockwise or shifted rightwards (from the viewpoint of the respective actor).
evidence: Describes the experimental design

claim: The mean manipulation duration was larger in trials with non-informative cues compared to informative cues in both monkeys.
source: Accordingly, we found a larger mean manipulation duration in trials with non-informative as compared to informative cues in both monkeys (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: There was a difference in the mean approach duration between the three actions in both monkeys.
source: Consistent with this incidential observation, we found a difference in the mean approach duration between the three actions in both monkeys (Figure 1E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: There was a difference in the mean approach duration between the three actions for the human actor.
source: Consistent with this incidential observation, we found a difference in the mean approach duration between the three actions in both monkeys (Figure 1E) and the human actor (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The monkey's gaze was slightly offset from the object's center but did not differ between the three actions.
source: We found that the monkey's gaze was slightly offset from the object's center (horizontal offset (dva): –1.6±1.2 in lift, –1.7±1.2 in twist, –1.7±1.3 in shift [mean ± std across sessions of both monkeys]; vertical offset (dva): 0.2±0.9 in lift, 0.0±1.0 in twist, 0.0±1.0 in shift), but did not differ between the three actions (MANOVA: Wilks' Lambda = 0.98, F(2, 375)=1.65, p=0.81).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: 240 neurons were recorded from two monkeys, of which 177 (74%) met the mirror neuron criteria.
source: We recorded 240 neurons from two monkeys, of which 177 (74%) met the mirror neuron criteria outlined in Material and methods and were used for the following analyses.
evidence: Describes the experimental data collected

claim: Many mirror neurons discharged dependent on the type of action being observed.
source: Many, but not all, mirror neurons (MNs) discharged dependent on the type of action being observed.
evidence: Describes the experimental findings

claim: The dependence of the discharge rate on the observed action often existed only at certain times of the action.
source: This dependence of the discharge rate on the observed action often existed only at certain times of the action.
evidence: Describes the experimental findings

claim: For some neurons, the relationship between the discharge rate and the type of action observed depended on time.
source: Moreover, for some neurons, the relationship between the discharge rate and the type of action observed, that is, the code for observed actions, also depended on time.
evidence: Describes the experimental findings

claim: The percentage of mirror neurons encoding observed actions ranged from 0 to 45% depending on the time bin.
source: The percentage of MNs encoding observed actions ranged from 0 to 45% depending on the time bin (green in Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Of the total 2124 bins tested, 22% (n=458) encoded observed actions.
source: Of the total 2124 bins tested (12 bins * 177 MNs), 22% (n=458, Figure 3A and B) encoded observed actions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: In 60% of the n=458 bins that encoded the actions on observation, the actions were also encoded on execution.
source: In 60% of the n=458 bins that encoded the actions on observation, the actions were also encoded on execution (n=274, Exe & Obs, yellow in Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: 72% of mirror neurons (n=128, 53% of F5 neurons examined) encoded the observed actions in at least one bin.
source: The bins in which observed actions were discriminated were distributed across all 177 MNs examined such that 72% of MNs (n=128, 53% of F5 neurons examined) encoded the observed actions in at least one bin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: Using the same discharge method, about 10% (n=28) of the bins examined (n=274) exhibited a shared code.
source: Of the bins examined (n=274), about 10% (n=28) exhibited such a shared code (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Using the same preference method, 31% (n=84) of the bins examined (n=274) had a shared code.
source: Using this method, of the bins examined (n=274), 31% (n=84) had a shared code (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Using the cross-task classification method, 23% (n=64) of the bins examined (n=274) had a shared code.
source: Of the bins examined (n=274), 23% (n=64) turned out to have a shared code (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The proportion of bins with a shared code using the same preference method is higher than would be expected by chance according to the null hypothesis.
source: This proportion is higher than to be expected by chance according to the aforementioned null hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with null hypothesis

claim: All three methods document that the overwhelming majority (about 80–95%) of bins in which action-related information is encoded when observed do not have a shared code.
source: Hence, all three methods document that the overwhelming majority (about 80–95%) of bins in which action-related information is encoded when observed do not have a shared code.
evidence: Summarizes findings from the three methods of analysis

claim: Almost all bins with significant accuracy of observed actions with an e2o classifier fell into a cluster where the accuracy was nearly the same for e2o and o2o classifiers.
source: Almost all the previously mentioned bins that had a significant accuracy of observed actions with a e2o classifier (n=64) fell into this group (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Only three neurons using the preference method or two neurons using the LDA method exhibited exclusively shared bins.
source: Only three (Pref method) or two (LDA method) of these neurons exhibited exclusively shared bins, and the neurons differed depending on the method (IDs 44, 154, 96 for Pref, IDs 9, 84 for LDA).
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: Almost all mirror neurons that encode observed actions with a shared code do so only at certain times, but encode the actions differently at other times.
source: This means that almost all MNs that encode observed actions with a shared code do so only at certain times, but encode the actions differently at other times.
evidence: Based on inference from the data on neurons with shared and non-shared bins

claim: Observed actions were discriminated later by execution-trained classifiers than by observation-trained classifiers.
source: It is confirmed that (1) observed actions were discriminated later by execution-trained classifiers (red in Figure 6) than by observation-trained classifiers (green)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: Observed actions were discriminated best by observation-trained classifiers after reaching the target position of the object.
source: and (2) observed actions were discriminated best by observation-trained classifiers after reaching the target position of the object.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: For both types of within-task classifiers, e2e and o2o, higher accuracies were achieved with an optimal value of 100% in the bin where the target object position was reached.
source: Accordingly, for both types of within-task classifiers, e2e and o2o, higher accuracies were achieved with an optimal value of 100% in the bin where the target object position was reached (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The anatomical locations of neurons with only shared bins and those with only non-shared bins were largely overlapped.
source: As shown in Figure 7, the anatomical locations of these two subpopulations were largely overlapped.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7

claim: Three observed actions performed on visually identical objects were well discriminated in the whole population of F5 mirror neurons studied.
source: In summary, we showed that three observed actions performed on visually identical objects and differing in the required grip type, manipulation type, and the object's target position were well discriminated in the whole population of F5 MNs studied.
evidence: Summarizes the main experimental findings

claim: Discrimination of observed actions began during approach to the object, at a time when the actions became discriminable.
source: Discrimination began during approach to the object, at a time when the actions became discriminable, and it was optimal when the object's target position had been reached.
evidence: Summarizes the main experimental findings

claim: Discrimination of observed actions was optimal when the object's target position had been reached.
source: Discrimination began during approach to the object, at a time when the actions became discriminable, and it was optimal when the object's target position had been reached.
evidence: Summarizes the main experimental findings

claim: The action-specific activity states of the whole population during observation were to some extent similar to the states during the execution of corresponding actions.
source: While the action-specific activity states of the whole population during observation were – to some extent – similar to the states during the execution of corresponding actions, they were not similar enough to allow the observed actions to be decoded as well by linear classifiers trained on action execution as by those trained on action observation.
evidence: Summarizes the main experimental findings

claim: There were time bins in up to about 20% of mirror neurons in which observed actions were discriminated equally well by observation- and execution-trained classifiers.
source: In contrast to the demonstration of such non-shared population codes in the whole population, analyses of the single neurons revealed that there were time bins in up to about 20% of MNs in which observed actions were discriminated equally well by observation- and execution-trained classifiers.
evidence: Summarizes the main experimental findings

claim: Time bins with shared code were rare and co-occurred with non-shared code bins in most neurons.
source: While these time bins with shared code were rare and co-occurred with non-shared code bins in most neurons, they formed a distinct cluster and are not to be considered random.
evidence: Summarizes the main experimental findings

claim: Time bins with shared code formed a distinct cluster and are not to be considered random.
source: While these time bins with shared code were rare and co-occurred with non-shared code bins in most neurons, they formed a distinct cluster and are not to be considered random.
evidence: Summarizes the main experimental findings

claim: The accuracies of shared population codes for subpopulations were worse than those of the non-shared population codes for the whole population.
source: However, the accuracies of such shared population codes for subpopulations were worse than those of the non-shared population codes for the whole population.
evidence: Summarizes the main experimental findings

claim: The finding of a low proportion of mirror neurons with shared codes is similar to the finding of a proportion of 5.5% 'strictly congruent' mirror neurons reported by Gallese et al., 1996.
source: Our finding of a low proportion of MNs with shared codes is similar to the finding of a proportion of 5.5% 'strictly congruent' MNs relative to the F5 neurons studied (29/531) reported by Gallese et al., 1996.
evidence: Compares current findings with previous study by Gallese et al., 1996

claim: The proportion of mirror neurons with shared code relative to all F5 neurons ranged from 0.8% to 16% depending on the criteria used.
source: In our study, depending on the criteria used, the proportion of MNs with shared code relative to all F5 neurons ranged from 0.8% to 16% (from 2/240 MNs with only bins with a shared code using the cross-task classification method up to 38/240 MNs with at least one bin with a shared code using the preference method).
evidence: Summarizes the experimental findings with different analysis methods

claim: The proportion of 'incongruent' neurons forms the clear majority.
source: However, the crucial difference to Gallese et al. is that we found that the proportion of 'incongruent' neurons, that is, neurons without bins with shared coding, is not below 10%, but forms the clear majority.
evidence: Summarizes the experimental findings

claim: Most mirror neurons that are classifiable as 'congruent' based on the occurrence of at least one bin with a shared code also contain bins with a non-shared code.
source: Moreover, most MNs that are classifiable as 'congruent' based on the occurrence of at least one bin with a shared code also contain bins with a non-shared code.
evidence: Summarizes the experimental findings

claim: The finding that mirror neurons discriminate observed actions well by non-shared codes is in line with a recent report by Papadourakis and Raos (2019).
source: Our finding that MNs discriminate observed actions well by non-shared codes is in line with a recent report by Papadourakis and Raos (2019), who tested the coding of actions that differed in the type of grip afforded by the object being grasped.
evidence: Compares current findings with previous study by Papadourakis and Raos (2019)

claim: The activity of F5 mirror neurons during action observation is not a supramodal motor representation of the observed action, as if the observer were performing it in place of the actor.
source: Our finding is evidence against the representation hypothesis, which is based on a strictly defined mirror mechanism. That is to say, the activity of F5 MNs, as defined by Gallese et al., 1996, during action observation is not a supramodal motor representation of the observed action, as if the observer were performing it in place of the actor.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental findings

claim: The representation hypothesis might hold for a subset of F5 mirror neurons, yet only for restricted segments of an action.
source: At best, the representation hypothesis might hold for a subset of F5 MNs, yet only for restricted segments of an action (see below).
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental findings

claim: The prerequisite for the understanding hypothesis is not met for the whole population of F5 mirror neurons.
source: Therefore, the prerequisite for the understanding hypothesis is not met for the whole population of F5 MNs.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental findings

claim: About 20% of the mirror neurons that contained time bins with shared code met the requirement for a motor representation according to the strictly defined mirror mechanism in these time bins.
source: In contrast to the whole population of F5 MNs, about 20% of the MNs in our study that contained time bins with shared code met the requirement for a motor representation according to the strictly defined mirror mechanism in these time bins.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental findings

claim: F5 mirror neurons may comprise functionally different subsets with some serving shared coding at particular times.
source: That F5 MNs may comprise functionally different subsets of MNs with some serving shared coding at particular times may not be implausible given that they differ in their anatomic location and connections (Kraskov et al., 2009) as well as their cellular identity (Ferroni et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kraskov et al., 2009 and Ferroni et al., 2021

claim: F5 mirror neurons differ in how they modulate during the execution or observation of actions and whether or not certain factors influence them.
source: Consistent with this, F5 MNs differ in how they modulate during the execution or observation of actions and whether or not certain factors influence them (Caggiano et al., 2011; Maranesi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caggiano et al., 2011 and Maranesi et al., 2013

claim: Simulating decoders that time-dependently read from the population of mirror neurons with shared code did not achieve the performance of decoders that read from the whole population.
source: First, simulating decoders that time-dependently read from the population of MNs with shared code did not achieve the performance of decoders that read from the whole population.
evidence: Summarizes the experimental findings

claim: The comparison of the duration and starting position of the segments with shared and non-shared codes did not provide convincing evidence that segments with shared code represent specific action aspects.
source: Second, the comparison of the duration and starting position of the segments with shared and non-shared codes did not provide convincing evidence that segments with shared code represent specific action aspects.
evidence: Summarizes the experimental findings

claim: There is as yet no evidence that the neurons of subpopulations with shared code act together on a target.
source: Third, there is as yet no evidence that the neurons of such subpopulations act together on a target.
evidence: Based on lack of evidence from the experimental findings

claim: The overwhelming majority of F5 mirror neurons encoded observed actions in a non-shared manner at most times.
source: The fact is that the overwhelming majority of F5 MNs encoded observed actions in a non-shared manner at most times.
evidence: Summarizes the experimental findings

claim: Neural responses of F5 neurons to a visual stimulus represent not the sensory properties of the stimulus itself, but the possible or upcoming action.
source: In terms of action execution, neural responses of F5 neurons to a visual stimulus such as the presentation of an object have been shown to represent not the sensory properties of the stimulus itself, but the possible or upcoming action, for example, the way of grasping the object afforded by the object properties (Schaffelhofer and Scherberger, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schaffelhofer and Scherberger, 2016

claim: Many F5 mirror neurons are influenced by the observer's reachability to the observed action.
source: With respect to action observation, findings that many F5 MNs are influenced by the observer's reachability to the observed action (Caggiano et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Caggiano et al., 2009

claim: Many F5 mirror neurons are influenced by the expected value of the goal for the observer.
source: and by the expected value of the goal for the observer (Pomper et al., 2020) show that the activity of many F5 MNs cannot be explained by this 'sensory concept'.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pomper et al., 2020

claim: The activity of F5 mirror neurons depends on whether the observer can reach the observed action.
source: This concept is supported by the findings that the activity of F5 MNs depends on whether the observer can reach the observed action (Caggiano et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Caggiano et al., 2009

claim: The activity of F5 mirror neurons depends on how much reward the observer can expect after the action.
source: and how much reward the observer can expect after the action (Caggiano et al., 2012; Pomper et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caggiano et al., 2012 and Pomper et al., 2020

claim: Viewpoint-invariant encoding of an observed action has been shown in a subset of F5 mirror neurons.
source: First, viewpoint-invariant encoding of an observed action has been shown in a subset of F5 MNs (Caggiano et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caggiano et al., 2011

claim: The similarity of state transitions between execution and observation was found by Mazurek et al., 2018.
source: Second, since the temporal sequence of intermediate goals is the same during execution and observation, the similarity of state transitions between execution and observation found by Mazurek et al., 2018 can be explained if a state transition is interpreted as achievement of an intermediate goal and the activation of a subsequent intermediate goal.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mazurek et al., 2018

claim: The expected goal value determines how well the monkey observes the action.
source: Third, that the monkey really pursues his own goal when observing is supported by the finding that the expected goal value determines how well he observes the action (Pomper et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pomper et al., 2020

claim: Some mirror neurons are influenced by the reachability and spatial configuration of the observed action.
source: Fourth, the preparedness to act on one's own to achieve the goal in the case of the other's failure explains why some MNs are influenced by the reachability and spatial configuration of the observed action (Caggiano et al., 2011; Caggiano et al., 2009; Maranesi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caggiano et al., 2011; Caggiano et al., 2009; Maranesi et al., 2017

claim: Information about the expected goal value for the observer is contained in F5 mirror neurons.
source: Fifth, it is consistent with the representation of a goal pursuit during observation that information about the expected goal value for the observer is contained in F5 MNs (Pomper et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pomper et al., 2020

claim: Monkeys with bilateral lesions of the subset of F5 neurons that project to the medial prefrontal cortex have an action goal selection deficit.
source: Sixth, and most importantly, this information about the expected goal value explains the action goal selection deficit of monkeys with bilateral lesions of the subset of F5 neurons that project to the medial prefrontal cortex (Ninomiya et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ninomiya et al., 2020

claim: Monkeys with lesions of F5 neurons projecting to medial prefrontal cortex were less able to detect 'choice errors' of the observed actor.
source: Monkeys with such lesions were less able to detect 'choice errors' of the observed actor.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ninomiya et al., 2020 mentioned in context

claim: F5 neurons are necessary for mapping the visual input of the observed action to an observer's own action goal and its expected value.
source: Thus, the study of Ninomyia et al. clearly shows that F5 neurons are neccessary for this mapping and/or the updating of the action goal value based on this mapping.
evidence: Based on inference from the Ninomiya et al. study

claim: The activity of some F5 mirror neurons during execution depends on whether the action is performed in darkness or in light.
source: This account seems to be supported by the finding that the activity of some F5 MNs during execution depends on whether the action is performed in darkness or in light (Maranesi et al., 2015).
